title: Designing a personal finance app

facts.text: The service must let a user connect a financial account, extract its transactions, categorize them (with manual category override but no automatic re-categorization), and analyze monthly spending by category.

It also recommends a budget the user may set manually, and sends notifications when spending approaches or exceeds the budget. It must be highly available; additional logging and analytics are out of scope.

Assumptions: traffic is not evenly distributed, adding or removing accounts is rare, budget notifications need not be instant, sellers determine a transaction's category, and the automatic daily update covers only users active in the past 30 days.

Scale: 10 million users, 30 million financial accounts, 10 budget categories per user (100 million budget items), 50,000 sellers, 5 billion transactions per month, 500 million read requests per month, and a 10:1 write to read ratio.
A transaction is about 50 bytes (user_id 8, created_at 5, seller 32, amount 5), so 5 billion a month means 250 GB of new transaction content per month and 9 TB in 3 years.
The average load is 2,000 transactions per second and 200 read requests per second. The system is write-heavy: users make transactions daily, but few visit the site daily.

To connect an account, the client calls a reverse-proxy web server, which forwards to the Accounts API server; that server writes the account to the SQL accounts table, indexed on id, user_id and created_at. The API is public REST.
Extraction runs when the user first links an account, on manual refresh, and daily for users active in the past 30 days. It takes a while, so the API server queues a job on Amazon SQS or RabbitMQ.

The Transaction Extraction Service pulls from the queue, stores raw transaction logs in an object store, calls the Category and Budget Services (the latter alerts users through a Notification Service), and updates the SQL transactions and monthly_spending tables.

The Category Service seeds a seller-to-category dictionary with popular sellers: 50,000 sellers at under 255 bytes each take about 12 MB of memory. Unseeded sellers are crowdsourced from user overrides, with a heap giving the top override in O(1).
Budgets start from a generic template that allocates category amounts by income tier, so the 100 million budget items need not be stored: only a user's overrides, in a budget_overrides table.

Monthly spending can come from SQL queries over transactions into monthly_spending, which has far fewer rows than 5 billion transactions. Alternatively, MapReduce jobs on the raw transaction files categorize and aggregate, reducing database load.

A memory cache such as Redis or Memcached holds sessions, category stats and recent transactions. The Read API server returns hits, else reads the SQL database and updates the cache (cache-aside). Static content comes from a CDN-cached object store.

The 200 average read requests per second (higher at peak) should be served by the cache, which also absorbs uneven traffic and spikes; SQL read replicas handle cache misses unless bogged down replicating writes.
2,000 average writes per second might be tough for a single SQL write master-slave, so add federation, denormalization and SQL tuning, and consider moving some data to NoSQL.
Keep only a month of transactions in the database and the rest in a data warehouse or object store; an object store such as Amazon S3 comfortably handles 250 GB of new content per month.
